intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 (LDS5), also known as Rienhoff syndrome, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TGFB3 gene (190230) on chromosome 14q24.3.

checks.evidence_quote: contribute to the clinical delineation of the emerging connective tissue disorder tentatively called Rienhoff syndrome
checks.explanation: The abstract uses the name Rienhoff syndrome (only as a tentative name) but never uses the designation Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5.

checks.evidence_quote: The proband was heterozygous for two de novo mutations.

paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder whose features overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Reported features include hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity and kyphoscoliosis, together with aortic aneurysm and dissection and mitral valve disease (Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015). Clinical variability is striking both within and between families. Some patients have tall stature, while others have growth retardation and low muscle mass (Rienhoff et al., 2013), and some affected families have no cardiovascular involvement (Kuechler et al., 2015).

checks.claim: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: We studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping with MFS and LDS consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
checks.explanation: The paper describes autosomal dominant inheritance of a disorder with connective tissue features.

checks.claim: The features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: a failure of normal post-natal muscle development without evidence of vascular disease; some features overlap with MFS and LDS.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European American girl whose parents were healthy and nonconsanguineous. At birth she had distal arthrogryposis, with contractures of the right hand (most severe in the 3rd and 4th fingers) and of all toes. She also had a midline facial nevus flammeus and mild hypotonia. She failed to thrive and her gross motor development was delayed. At 17 months she had hypertelorism, prominent eyes, blue sclerae, a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate, retrognathia, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus and hyperextensible large joints. She also had reduced muscle bulk with low tone and diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. She walked at 24 months with a waddling gait and a positive Gowers sign, and her neurocognitive development was normal. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. Her growth retardation persisted, and at age 7 she weighed below the 1st centile. Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months showed no cardiac defect, and her aortic root dimensions were normal (z score 0.39 at age 6.5 years). A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 showed only mild focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse, with no dystrophic or inflammatory changes.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with an autosomal dominant disorder whose features overlapped with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven members, aged 40 to 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died of aortic dissection and rupture. Four had mitral valve abnormalities ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation. Other features were subtle craniofacial changes (long face, high-arched palate, retrognathia), pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices and hiatal hernia. Autoimmune features included HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease and celiac disease.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) summarized 43 patients (23 male, 20 female) from 11 families with TGFB3 mutations, whose features overlapped with Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Four patients had type A dissection (median age 51 years) and 6 had type B dissection (median age 44.5 years). Other findings were aortic aneurysm, mitral valve disease, septal defects, hypertelorism, bifid uvula, cleft palate, cervical spine instability, clubfoot, tall stature, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, kyphoscoliosis, joint hypermobility and hernia. The authors observed no early dissection, no dissection at small aortic size, no striking arterial tortuosity and no ectopia lentis. Clinical variability was striking both within and between families.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) studied a girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass and growth retardation. Exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous c.1226G-A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant was de novo, and it was not present in dbSNP130, the EVS database or 1000 Genomes. No mutations were found in TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, FBN1 or FBN2. In functional studies, secreted mutant TGFB3 failed to activate a TGF-beta reporter. In Xenopus embryos, co-injection of mutant and wildtype RNA reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signaling, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. The same patient carried a de novo heterozygous nonsense variant in CDH2 (c.208C-T, Q70X). N-cadherin levels in her fibroblasts were normal, and Cdh2-null heterozygous mice are normal, so the authors concluded that this variant was unlikely to drive the phenotype. They could not exclude modifying effects.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) found a heterozygous splice donor mutation in intron 4 of the TGFB3 gene (c.754+2T-C) in affected members of the Dutch family 1. The mutation segregated with the phenotype and was absent from variant databases. Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) then screened 470 additional probands with syndromic or nonsyndromic TAAD, 350 by Sanger sequencing and 120 by exome sequencing. They found heterozygous TGFB3 mutations in 10 more probands: 4 different missense mutations, 1 nonsense mutation and 2 single-base deletions causing frameshifts. None of the mutations was present in controls in EVS, 1000 Genomes or Genome of the Netherlands. The proband of family 6 had a de novo nonsense mutation (Y365X). This proband also carried a SMAD3 variant of unknown significance (A250T), inherited from a mother who had variable connective tissue findings and mild cardiovascular involvement; the authors considered its contribution unclear.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) used exome sequencing to study a European American girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass and growth retardation. They identified a de novo heterozygous c.1226G-A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution. Cys409 is the penultimate cysteine of the cysteine knot and is conserved across TGF-beta family ligands. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variant was de novo, and it was absent from dbSNP130, the EVS database and 1000 Genomes. Secreted mutant TGFB3 failed to activate a TGF-beta reporter in cultured cells. In Xenopus embryos, co-injection of mutant and wildtype RNA at a 1:1 ratio reduced pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signals to about 40% and 60% of wildtype levels, respectively, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. The mutant had no effect on BMP/SMAD1 signaling. The authors concluded that the mutation is hypomorphic.

checks.claim: Kuechler et al. (2015) noted that a different mutation at TGFB3 codon 300 (R300Q) had previously been reported in a child with overgrowth.
checks.evidence_quote: a child with overgrowth carried a mutation in the same codon as the mutation identified in the three affected individuals reported here (c.899G>A; p.Arg300Gln; Matyas et al., 2014)

checks.claim: Kuechler et al. (2015) suggested that TGFB3 arg300 mutations presumably increase TGF-beta signaling.
checks.evidence_quote: The mutations at codon Arg300 presumably lead to increased TGF-beta signalling
